User guide

slicekit guide

A closed-loop framework for spec-driven development with coding agents.

This guide has one page for every slicekit command, every /slicekit slash command and every check rule. A command's page gives its usage, what it reads and writes, its exit codes and an example; a check rule's page says what fails and the failure the rule prevents. This index links the pages and holds what no single page does: the stages from intake to release and the conventions the pages share.

Overview

The guide covers the slicekit command-line interface and the slash commands that drive it from Claude Code. A person types the slash commands; each one's procedure runs the CLI commands. Where the agent, CI or a Claude Code hook usually runs a command, the first lines of its page under Commands say so.

In your project the kit runs as npx slicekit, or through the cli value in .slicekit/config.json. With a local install that is node node_modules/slicekit/bin/slicekit.js. The examples write it as slicekit. Run every command from the repository root.

Stages

A program moves through these stages in this order. A stage command refuses to start until the files show the stage before it is complete. slicekit stage require <stage> is that check at the start of specify, gaps and build; plan uses slicekit plan check, and release uses slicekit release P<n> --dry-run. The stage names in the code are intake, clarify, specify, spec-review, gap-scan, stack, plan, build and release. Merging a pull request is always a person's act.

StageSlash commandWhat happensCLI steps
SetupOnce per repository. Adds the config, docs layout, Claude Code files, git hooks and the CI workflow.init, status --write, workflow --write
1. Intake/slicekit intake <file or URL>The source document is snapshotted and frozen. The agent asks one question at a time, and each answer becomes a numbered decision row.branch spec, intake snapshot, intake ask, intake answer, intake done, workflow --write
2. Clarifyno command of its ownQuestions intake left open are answered. The stage is complete when decisions.md exists and the spec cites no blocking Open row. An open row of type Action or Information is listed as pending and does not block.decide settle, decide add
3. Specify, then spec review/slicekit specifyOne spec file per capability, every requirement citing its source, a contract per interface. Then the spec pull request; merging it is the spec review.branch spec, stage require clarify, spec verify, check, pr open
4. Gaps/slicekit gapsAfter the spec merges: every place the spec is silent, vague or in conflict with intake becomes a G row, and each row is closed by a decision or a requirement change.branch gaps, stage require spec-review, gaps scan, instructions auditor, gaps add, decide settle, decide add, gaps close, gaps verify, check, pr open
5. Plan/slicekit planThe stack, the phases and the slice files, then BUILD.md and the plan pull request.branch plan, plan check, decide add, status --write, check, pr open
6. Build/slicekit build [P<n>/S-<nn>]One slice: start, failing tests, code until green, a draft pull request, at most two review rounds, green CI. Side by side: /slicekit build --parallel P<n> uses build parallel. Occasional: build amend, build render, build config, build sync.stage require plan, build next, build start, instructions developer, build red, build commit, build pr, instructions reviewer, build verdict, instructions fixer, build decline, build finish
7. Independent review, then merge/slicekit review <PR>In a new Claude Code session with no memory of the build. On blockers, and when the person says yes, a fixer's commits go to the slice branch. When it reports ready, a person merges. The CI sync job then runs status --sync --write and journal heads, and sync open opens a [sync] pull request; when a person merges that one, the slice is merged on the default branch.review start, instructions reviewer, build verdict --independent, instructions fixer, build decline, build commit --require-green, build pr, build sync, build finish; then in CI status --sync --write, journal heads, sync open
8. Release/slicekit release P<n>Once every slice of the phase is merged: writes the release record releases/P<n>.md, sets each slice released, rewrites BUILD.md and opens the [release] P<n> pull request. release --undo removes a record that is not committed, when check finds a fault in it. It does not deploy.release --dry-run, branch release, release, check, release --undo, pr open
9. The graph and its queriesany timeBuild the traceability graph from the docs and git, then ask it questions.graph, trace, impact, history, shipped, uncovered, visualize
10. Ops and audit/slicekit ops <symptom>, /slicekit audit [area]Any time after the first merge. Ops triages a symptom; audit compares the spec and runbook claims with the code. Each leaves one report and changes no tracked file.graph, ops context, instructions ops, ops check, audit context, instructions auditor, audit check --every-claim

Command groups

The table under Commands lists the pages by name. This section lists them by the work they belong to, with what the commands of a group share.

Setup

Adding the kit to a repository and keeping its own files current: init, update and workflow.

Intake and spec

The steps of /slicekit intake, /slicekit specify and /slicekit gaps: branch, intake, decide, stage, spec, gaps and pr. The agent runs nearly all of them. You type decide and stage require yourself now and then.

Plan

plan holds one step, plan check. /slicekit plan also runs branch plan, decide add, status --write, check and pr open.

Build loop

build holds the deterministic steps that /slicekit build and /slicekit review share, and instructions prints the brief of each agent they spawn. Each build subcommand but build next and build parallel takes the slice ID, P<n>/S-<nn>. A slice's worktree is .worktrees/P<n>-S-<nn> on the branch slice/P<n>-S-<nn>-<descr>. The agent runs every step; you type one only to resume or inspect by hand.

Shared by the build subcommands. --worktree <p> names the worktree to act in. Without it the build worktree is used, never the review one, so the building session needs no flag while a review session runs; the review session always passes it. Exit codes: 0 done; 1 refused (the slice's state, a failing command or check, a frozen test, a state file hidden from git or changed on disk, git, the git host, the tracker or a held lock); 2 bad usage, an unknown slice ID, a missing required option or a config problem.

Review and release

/slicekit review <PR> starts with review start, then uses the build steps with --worktree <wt>: build verdict --independent, build decline, build commit --require-green and build pr for a fix, build sync and build finish. release writes a phase's release record once every slice of the phase is merged.

CI and hooks

The gate, and the commands the generated workflow and Claude Code's hooks call: check, ci, ready-label, sync and hook. You type check often; the other four you would rarely type.

The graph and queries

graph builds .slicekit/graph/graph.json from the kit's IDs and from git: requirements, decisions, slices, tests, commits, pull requests and releases. It is not a code graph. The five queries, trace, impact, history, shipped and uncovered, read only that file; they run no git and no host call. visualize shows the same file as one page.

Shared by the five queries. --json prints one JSON document, also on an error ({"error": …}). Exit codes: 0 answered; 1 no graph (run slicekit graph), a graph of an older schema, or for shipped a phase with no release record; 2 bad usage, an ID or path not in the graph, or a config problem.

Maintenance

The slices' state, the ratchet baselines and the session journal: status, state, baseline and journal.

Ops and audit

The steps of /slicekit ops and /slicekit audit that the CLI takes: ops and audit. Each has a context step, which prints what the agent is handed, and a check step, which judges the report.

Conventions

Global options

  • slicekit --help: Prints the usage of every command on standard output and exits 0, so slicekit --help | less shows it. An unknown command prints the usage on standard error and exits 2.
  • slicekit <command> --help: Prints that command's usage on standard output and exits 0, for example slicekit build --help.
  • slicekit --version: Prints the installed version on standard output and exits 0.

Help

Every command takes --help: slicekit build --help prints the usage of build and its subcommands and exits 0. Running slicekit with no command, or an unknown one, prints the usage of every command and exits 2.

A value that starts with a dash

Write it as --option=<text>, with the equals sign. Otherwise the value is read as another option. This holds for every option; the procedures always use this form for free text.

$ slicekit decide settle D-09 --answer="-1 means no limit" --type Decision

Exit codes

CodeMeaning
0Success. For a gate, the thing checked is ready or clean.
1Refused or not ready: a finding, a blocker, a state the step does not run from, or git, the git host or the tracker said no. The message says what to fix.
2Cannot run: bad usage, an unknown ID, slice, stage or role, or a missing or invalid .slicekit/config.json.

Five commands differ on purpose: ci bookkeeping and ready-label exit 0 whatever they decide, hook exits 0 for every known hook and puts its decision in the JSON, baseline show exits 0 even when a baseline file is damaged, and status has no exit 1: it exits 2 for a git host error too.

A held lock on a state file is exit 2 for state and status, and exit 1 for build. Each page's Exit codes section is the full list for its command.

Config version

.slicekit/config.json carries configVersion. A config with an older one is migrated on the first command that is not hook: the file is written once and each change is printed on stderr. A hook reads the config as migrated and writes nothing. A configVersion newer than the kit's is refused with a message naming both versions.

In two cases a command reads the config as migrated, writes nothing and prints one line on stderr saying the config is at the older version and is read as the newer one, unwritten (D-93, D-94):

  • slicekit branch, of every kind, because it refuses a changed tracked file. The branch is cut first, and the next command writes the migration on it.
  • Every command on a slice branch or a slice's review branch, because no build step commits a config change there. The slice whose Expected changes name .slicekit/config.json is the exception; its slice branch and its review branch are written and slicekit build config commits the change.

A team commits the migration on a plan branch with three commands, run from the default branch after the newer kit is installed:

  1. slicekit branch plan <slug> cuts the branch and leaves the config as it is.
  2. Any command that is not hook or branch, for example slicekit status, writes the migrated config there and prints each change.
  3. slicekit pr open --title <title> --body-file <file> --commit <message> --paths .slicekit/config.json commits it and opens the pull request, which a human reviews and merges.

If another command ran on the default branch first, for example slicekit release P<n> --dry-run, the config is already written there. slicekit branch, of every kind, still cuts the branch when the only uncommitted change to a tracked file is the config and it equals what the migration writes from the committed config; the change is carried to the new branch, where pr open commits it. Where the branch already holds the migrated config, with equal content, slicekit branch drops its own copy of the change and switches; where the branch holds a config that differs, it exits 1 with one line naming the file, the branch and the fields that differ, and the change is left where it is. Any other uncommitted change is refused with commit or stash your changes first. A kit before config version 2 refuses a migrated config with configVersion: must be 1.

Other conventions

  • Slice IDs are P<n>/S-<nn>, for example P1/S-02. Decisions are D-<n>, gaps G-<n>, blockers B-<n>, should-haves H-<n>, contracts C-<n>.
  • The commands own git. The developer, the fixer, the reviewer and the auditor write files and report; the ops agent holds read tools only, and its reply is the report. The CLI commits, pushes and opens pull requests. The pre-bash hook refuses git writes from a subagent.
  • The git host is GitHub through the gh CLI. SLICEKIT_GITHOST_FIXTURE and SLICEKIT_TRACKER_FIXTURE point the kit at fixture folders instead, as the README walkthrough does.
  • Where a command prints a path, it uses forward slashes on every platform.

Slash commands

/slicekit

Runs any of the ten procedures by name. It is the one slash command a person needs to remember.

What you type

/slicekit <command> [args], where the command is one of brief, intake, specify, gaps, plan, build, review, release, ops and audit. For example /slicekit build or /slicekit review 14. Each procedure also has a file of its own, so /slicekit-build is the same command as /slicekit build.

Agents it spawns

None of its own. The procedure it prints says which agents to spawn; see that procedure's page.

Commands its procedure runs
  • instructions as instructions --command <command> [args], then every command the printed procedure names.

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

What the named procedure leaves. The command file in .claude/commands/ holds no rule: it runs instructions --command and follows what prints, so an upgrade of the kit changes the procedure without changing the file.

Back to the guide

/slicekit brief

Interviews a person who has an idea but no requirement document, and writes the brief that /slicekit intake takes as its source.

What you type

/slicekit brief [<slug>]. Run it before /slicekit intake, when there is no requirement document yet. With no slug, the session asks the person for a short name for the idea.

Agents it spawns

None. The session itself asks the questions, one topic per question, in this order: the problem and who has it, what they do today, the use cases, what is out of scope, the success measures, the constraints, and the unknowns.

Commands its procedure runs
  • branch as branch spec <slug>
  • brief as brief start <slug>, then brief ask before each question and brief answer after each answer, then brief done

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The branch spec/<slug>. The brief <docsRoot>/brief/<slug>.md, committed, with the seven sections and only the person's answers; each topic the person could not answer is listed under ## Open questions. The next command, printed as the last line: /slicekit intake <docsRoot>/brief/<slug>.md. No spec file and no pull request.

Back to the guide

/slicekit intake

Brings a requirement document into the project and interviews the person about it.

What you type

/slicekit intake <file or URL>. Run it first, with the requirement document, and again for each new source.

Agents it spawns

None. The session itself asks the questions, one at a time: a product pass (purpose, users, components, existing systems, constraints, out of scope, interfaces), then a platform pass that fills platform.md and observability.md.

Commands its procedure runs
  • branch as branch spec <slug>
  • intake as intake snapshot, then intake ask before each question and intake answer after each answer, then intake done
  • workflow as workflow --write, after the table of CI steps in observability.md changes

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The branch spec/<slug>. A frozen snapshot of the source and its sidecar under <docsRoot>/intake/, committed. One decision row per answer in <docsRoot>/decisions.md, with platform.md and observability.md filled in, committed. The list of questions still open, printed. No spec file and no pull request.

Back to the guide

/slicekit specify

Writes the spec from the intake snapshots and the decisions, then opens the spec pull request.

What you type

/slicekit specify. Run it after intake, once the open questions are settled.

Agents it spawns

None. The session writes the spec files from the snapshots and the decision rows only. Where no source supports a claim it writes a [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: …] marker and does not guess.

Commands its procedure runs
  • branch as branch spec <slug>
  • stage as stage require clarify
  • spec as spec verify, until it exits 0
  • check
  • pr as pr open --title "[spec] <program name>"

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

One file per capability under <docsRoot>/spec/, each requirement citing its source, and one contract per interface named at intake under <docsRoot>/spec/contracts/. One commit and the [spec] <program name> pull request. Merging it approves the spec.

Back to the guide

/slicekit gaps

Finds each place where the spec is silent, vague or in conflict with the intake, asks the person about each, and closes every row.

What you type

/slicekit gaps. Run it after the spec pull request merges, before planning.

Agents it spawns

The auditor. Its brief is the output of instructions auditor. It reads the spec against the snapshots and the decisions, and records each gap a script cannot find.

Commands its procedure runs
  • branch as branch gaps <slug>
  • stage as stage require spec-review
  • gaps as gaps scan; the auditor runs gaps add; then gaps close per row and gaps verify
  • instructions as instructions auditor
  • decide as decide settle or decide add, for each answer
  • check
  • pr as pr open --title "[spec] <program name>: gaps"

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The gaps file <docsRoot>/spec/gaps.md with every row closed by a decision or a requirement change. New or settled decision rows. Answers written into platform.md, observability.md or the runbook in place of "Not yet known". One commit and the gaps pull request. When the person cannot answer a row yet, the row stays open and no pull request is opened.

Back to the guide

/slicekit plan

Writes the stack, the phases and the slice files from the spec, then opens the plan pull request.

What you type

/slicekit plan. Run it after the gaps pull request merges.

Agents it spawns

None. The session asks the person one question per stack choice the sources leave open.

Commands its procedure runs
  • branch as branch plan <slug>
  • plan as plan check
  • decide as decide add, for each stack choice
  • status as status --write, after each change to a slice file
  • check, until it reports 0 findings
  • pr as pr open --title "[plan] <program name>"

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The stack file <docsRoot>/spec/stack.md. One phase file per milestone with its **Order:** line, and the slice files beside it, each with its Done when list, its evaluation set and its expected changes. BUILD.md regenerated. One commit and the [plan] <program name> pull request. Merging it approves the plan.

Back to the guide

/slicekit build

Builds one slice from todo to a pull request ready for a person to merge: failing tests first, then code, at most two review rounds, then green CI.

What you type

/slicekit build, which takes the next slice; /slicekit build P<n>/S-<nn> for a named one; or /slicekit build --parallel P<n>, which starts every runnable slice of the phase's next Order step, each in its own worktree. Run it after the plan pull request merges, once per slice.

Agents it spawns

The developer, twice: first for the tests of the evaluation set, then for the code that makes them pass. The reviewer, once per round, which writes a verdict file. The fixer, when a verdict holds blockers or should-haves the person chose to fix. Each brief is the output of instructions <role> <id> --worktree <path>. The agents write files and report; they never commit or push.

Commands its procedure runs
  • stage as stage require plan
  • build as build next and build start, or build parallel; build red; build commit; build pr; build verdict; build decline for each should-have the person declines; build finish
  • build as build amend when a person agrees a frozen test may change, build render and build config for a slice that changes the kit's version or the config, and build sync when another worktree pushed to the slice branch
  • instructions as instructions developer, instructions reviewer and instructions fixer

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The worktree .worktrees/P<n>-S-<nn> on the branch slice/P<n>-S-<nn>-<descr>, pushed. The red commit of the frozen tests, then code commits, each with the Slice: trailer and the test run's result. The pull request [P<n>/S-<nn>] <name> with the body the kit requires. One verdict file per round under .slicekit/reviews/. One tracker issue per declined should-have. The slice at ci-green, waiting for the independent review, or at ready. A blocker that survives round two leaves the slice at changes-requested and the pull request a draft.

Back to the guide

/slicekit review

Gives a slice pull request its independent verdict, from a session that holds no context of the build.

What you type

/slicekit review <PR>, in a new Claude Code session, after /slicekit build reports ready: waiting for an independent review. The kit cannot check that the session is new; that is left to the person who starts it.

Agents it spawns

The reviewer, in a fresh worktree of the pull request's head, with the brief from instructions reviewer <id> --worktree <wt>. On blockers, and only when the person says yes, the fixer.

Commands its procedure runs
  • review as review start <PR>
  • instructions as instructions reviewer and, for a fix, instructions fixer
  • build with --worktree <wt>: build verdict --independent; build decline; for a fix build commit --require-green and build pr; build sync; build finish

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The review worktree .worktrees/review-P<n>-S-<nn>. A verdict file marked independent, committed and pushed to the slice branch; it does not count against the build's two rounds. After a fix, new commits on the slice branch and a new independent verdict on the new head. The slice at ready when CI is green and the verdict has no open blocker. A person merges.

Back to the guide

/slicekit release

Writes the release record of a phase whose slices are all merged, and opens the release pull request. It deploys nothing.

What you type

/slicekit release P<n>, after the last slice of the phase merges.

Agents it spawns

None.

Commands its procedure runs
  • release as release P<n> --dry-run, then release P<n>; release P<n> --undo when check finds a fault in the record
  • branch as branch release <slug>, the slug being the phase in lower case
  • check, until it reports 0 findings
  • pr as pr open --title "[release] P<n>"

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

The branch release/<slug>. The release record <docsRoot>/releases/P<n>.md, each slice of the phase at released, and BUILD.md rewritten, in one commit. The [release] P<n> pull request; merging it is the release of the phase in this repository. When a slice is not merged, has no recorded pull request or fails the runbook judgement, the dry run names it and nothing is written.

Back to the guide

/slicekit ops

Triages one symptom: the slices and pull requests that touched the files it names, the runbook's first checks, and the actions someone could take. It takes no action.

What you type

/slicekit ops <symptom>, for example /slicekit ops checkout returns 502. With no symptom it asks for one.

Agents it spawns

The ops agent, with the brief from instructions ops. It holds only read tools: no tool that writes a file or runs a command. Its reply is the report, and the session writes that reply to the report path unchanged.

Commands its procedure runs
  • graph, so the history holds the latest merged pull requests
  • ops as ops context "<symptom>", with --path <path> for each file the person names when the words match none
  • instructions as instructions ops
  • ops as ops check <report>; on findings the agent is sent back once

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

One report, .slicekit/reports/ops-<k>.md, with the sections Likely slices and pull requests, First checks and Proposed actions, each action marked by who may take it. The report folder is ignored by git, so no tracked file changes and nothing is committed. Each proposed action is the person's, or the named owner's, to take.

Back to the guide

/slicekit audit

Compares what the spec and the runbook claim with what the code, the tests and the CI history show.

What you type

/slicekit audit [area]. The area is a spec file's name without .md, a REQ prefix such as REQ-2, the word runbook, or a path. With no area, every claim is audited.

Agents it spawns

The auditor, in audit mode, with the brief from instructions auditor. It is given the claims and writes the report at the report path.

Commands its procedure runs
  • graph, so the files the claims name are read from the latest history
  • audit as audit context [area]
  • instructions as instructions auditor
  • audit as audit check <report> [area] --every-claim; on findings the auditor is sent back once

Every step that touches git or the git host goes through the CLI. The procedure stops at the first command that exits with a code other than 0 and shows the person its message.

What it leaves behind

One report, .slicekit/reports/audit-<k>.md, with a Claims table: one row per claim, its evidence, where it was found, and a status of holds, drifted or unverifiable. The report folder is ignored by git, so no tracked file changes. The audit changes nothing: each drifted row becomes a slice or a decision by a person's hand, and each unverifiable row is a claim with no test or check behind it.

Back to the guide

Commands

slicekit audit

The two steps of /slicekit audit that the CLI takes: the claims handed to the auditor, and the check of the report it writes.

Usage
slicekit audit context [area] [--all] [--no-report] [--json]slicekit audit check <report> [area] [--every-claim]

audit context [area] prints the report path on its first line. Then, for each claim of the area, it prints the claim's ID, its <file>:<line> and its title, a files: line naming the files the claim names, and one candidate <sha7> <date> <subject> line for each commit that touched one of those files after the claim's heading was last changed. A claim is a REQ block of the spec or a ## section of the runbook.

The area is a spec file's name without .md or its path, a REQ prefix such as REQ-2, one REQ ID, the word runbook, or a path. With no area, every claim is listed.

  • --all: prints every candidate. Without it a claim shows its ten newest candidates, then one line that counts the older ones and names the command that prints them: audit context <area> --all --no-report, written with the kit's command prefix (cli in the config).
  • --no-report: prints the context alone. No report path is printed and no report file is created. Use it with --all to read the older candidates of a claim during an audit; the report of that audit stays the one its first audit context created.
  • --json: prints one JSON document that holds every candidate. With --no-report its report is null.

audit check <report> [area] reads the area's claims again from the spec and the runbook and prints ok <report>, or one <report>:<line> <message> line per problem:

  • no ## Claims section, no table in it, or a table whose columns are not Claim, Where, Evidence, Found at, Status, Commit;
  • a row for a claim that is not in the area, or a second row for one claim;
  • a status that is not holds, drifted or unverifiable;
  • a drifted row whose commit is not one of the claim's candidates;
  • a missing Skipped: or Not checked: closing line;
  • with --every-claim, a claim of the area that has no row.
What it reads and writes

Reads the spec, the runbook, the graph file and git's history. audit context creates the empty report file .slicekit/reports/audit-<k>.md, which the ignore rules that init writes cover; with --no-report it creates none. audit check writes nothing. Neither changes a tracked file.

Exit codes
  • 0context: printed. check: the report has no problem
  • 1check: at least one problem. Either: no graph, a graph of an older schema, or a git error
  • 2bad usage, an unknown subcommand, an area that names no claim, a report path that is not a file, or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit audit context runbook
.slicekit/reports/audit-1.md
runbook#how-to-run-it docs/runbook.md:3 How to run it
  files: bin/slicekit.js
  candidate 8b41d07 2026-11-02 fix(cli): --help prints on stdout
$ slicekit audit context runbook --all --no-report
runbook#how-to-run-it docs/runbook.md:3 How to run it
  files: bin/slicekit.js
  candidate 8b41d07 2026-11-02 fix(cli): --help prints on stdout
$ slicekit audit check .slicekit/reports/audit-1.md runbook --every-claim
ok .slicekit/reports/audit-1.md

Back to the guide

slicekit baseline

Shows the ratchet baselines, or lowers them to today's counts.

Usage
slicekit baseline <update [--adopt]|show> [--json]

The ratchet rules are references and style. Each keeps one count per file; check fails a file whose count is above its baseline.

baseline update lowers each baseline to today's count. It refuses to raise one: baselines only go down.

  • --adopt: a first adoption in a repository that already has findings. It records higher counts and prints each with its previous value. It is refused when CI is set.
  • --json: prints written, refused, adopted, rewrote and problems as JSON.

baseline show prints the baselines as JSON, with or without --json. Problems with a baseline file go to stderr.

What it reads and writes

Reads the docs and the baseline files under .slicekit/baselines/. baseline update writes those files. baseline show writes nothing.

Exit codes
  • 0done or printed; baseline show exits 0 even when a baseline file is damaged
  • 1update: a raise was refused, or a baseline file is damaged
  • 2bad usage, --adopt in CI, or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit baseline update
baseline style docs/spec/refunds.md: 4 → 2

Back to the guide

slicekit branch

Puts the session on the work branch of a document pull request.

Usage
slicekit branch <spec|gaps|plan|release> <slug>

The branch is <kind>/<slug>. A new branch is cut from the default branch as origin has it, after a fetch. A branch that exists here or on origin is taken up where it stands. Untracked files go along; changes to tracked files are refused, with one exception, the migrated config below.

A release branch is treated differently. One that is behind the default branch's tip and holds no commit of its own is moved to that tip, and the command says so. One that holds its own commits is refused with one of three lines: the open pull request of that branch, a line saying the git host could not be asked, or the next slug to run the command with: the next free number of the slug's family, <slug>-2 or the first number after it that no branch here or on origin has. The git host is also asked about each numbered branch of the slug, release/<slug>-<n>, that holds commits the default branch lacks: an open pull request on any of them refuses, the line names that pull request and its branch, and no further slug is named. A numbered slug given directly, <slug>-<n> with <n> 2 or more, belongs to the same family: the host is asked about release/<slug> and every release/<slug>-<n>, and the next slug named is <slug>-<n+1> or the first number after it that is free, never <slug>-<n>-2.

The slug is the program name in lower case with other characters turned into dashes; for release it is the phase in lower case. It holds lowercase letters, digits and dashes, at most 60 characters, and does not start with a dash.

A migrated config

A kit with a newer config version migrates .slicekit/config.json on the first command that is not hook, and writes the file once (REQ-5.6). slicekit branch is one of the two cases where it does not (D-93):

  • slicekit branch, of every kind, reads an older config as migrated and writes nothing. It prints one config: line on stderr saying so. The branch is cut first, and the next command writes the migration on that branch, where pr open commits it.
  • The other case is every command on a slice branch or a slice's review branch, unless that slice's Expected changes name the config.

When an earlier command on the default branch, such as release --dry-run, already wrote the migrated config, it is an uncommitted change to a tracked file. slicekit branch does not refuse that one change (D-94). It applies when the config is the only uncommitted change to a tracked file and the file equals what the migration writes from the committed config:

The commit the session is put onWhat happens to the change
holds the config the current commit holdsit is carried to the branch, where pr open commits it
holds the migrated config already, with equal contentthis copy of the change is dropped, then the branch is switched to; the file then holds the bytes that commit holds
holds a config that differs from the migrated oneexit 1 with one line naming the file, the branch and the fields that differ; the change is left where it is and no branch is switched to

Two configs that differ only in their line endings or in whitespace at the end have equal content. After a dropped copy and the switch, git status --porcelain prints nothing for the config and nothing is staged.

Any other uncommitted change to a tracked file is refused with commit or stash your changes first.

What it reads and writes

Reads the config, the local branches and origin. It fetches, then creates or checks out the branch. It asks the git host only for a release branch, or another branch of its slug's family, that holds its own commits. It writes no config; it restores .slicekit/config.json to the committed one only in the second row of the table above, first to the current commit's and, after the switch, to the bytes the branch's commit holds.

Exit codes
  • 0prints the branch name
  • 1uncommitted changes to tracked files, a migrated config that differs from the one the branch holds, a git error, a release branch that holds commits the default branch lacks, or another branch of its slug's family with an open pull request
  • 2bad usage, a bad slug, or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit branch spec orders
spec/orders

Back to the guide

slicekit brief

The steps of /slicekit brief that the CLI takes: open the brief, record each question and its answer in the order of the topics, then commit the brief.

Usage
slicekit brief start <slug>slicekit brief ask --topic <problem|today|use-cases|out-of-scope|success-measures|constraints|unknowns> --question <q>slicekit brief answer (--answer <a> | --unknown)slicekit brief done
SubcommandWhat it does
brief start <slug>Writes <docsRoot>/brief/<slug>.md with its seven headings and prints its path. It refuses on the default branch or a protected branch, while another brief is under way, and when the file exists.
brief askRecords the question the agent is about to ask and prints question <n>. The topic is the one last asked or the next in the order of the usage line. It refuses a topic out of that order, and a new question while the last one has no answer.
brief answerWrites the answer just given under its topic's heading and prints the brief's path. --unknown lists the topic under ## Open questions instead, once, and writes nothing under its heading; a later answer on the topic takes it off ## Open questions. It refuses --unknown on a topic that already has an answer, naming brief answer --answer for the follow-up answer. An answer to unknowns goes under ## Open questions.
brief doneCommits the brief alone on the current branch, then prints its path and, as the last line, /slicekit intake <docsRoot>/brief/<slug>.md. It refuses when no brief is under way, while a question has no answer, on the default branch or a protected branch, while a topic was never asked and answered (an answer given with --unknown counts as answered), naming the first such topic, when the brief file is missing, while a heading is missing from the brief, and when a file under <docsRoot>/spec/ appeared, changed or was removed since brief start.

slicekit stage require brief refuses a brief in which a topic's section is empty and the topic is not listed under ## Open questions, naming the file and the section, so a brief edited by hand is held to the same rule.

What it reads and writes

Reads the brief session file in the worktree's git directory and the files under <docsRoot>/spec/, to compare them with the start. Writes <docsRoot>/brief/<slug>.md and the session file, and one commit: the brief's.

Exit codes
  • 0done; ask prints question <n>, done ends with the intake command
  • 1refused: a protected branch, a topic out of order, a question with no answer, --unknown on an answered topic, a topic never asked, a missing heading, a changed spec file
  • 2bad usage or bad input: an unknown topic, a bad slug, both or neither of --answer and --unknown
Example
$ slicekit brief start payments-retry
docs/brief/payments-retry.md
$ slicekit brief ask --topic=problem --question="What goes wrong, and for whom?"
question 1
$ slicekit brief answer --answer="Card payments that time out are lost; the support team handles them."
docs/brief/payments-retry.md
$ # one brief ask and one brief answer for each of the six other topics, in order
$ slicekit brief done
docs/brief/payments-retry.md
/slicekit intake docs/brief/payments-retry.md

Back to the guide

slicekit build

The steps of /slicekit build and /slicekit review that the CLI takes for one slice. The agent runs each; a person types one only to resume or inspect.

Usage
slicekit build next  | build start <id> [--descr <d>]  | build parallel P<n>  | build red <id> --tests <a,b> [--worktree <p>]  | build commit <id> --message <m> [--require-green] [--worktree <p>] (commits the staged paths; with nothing staged, every changed path)  | build render <id> [--worktree <p>]  | build config <id> [--worktree <p>]  | build amend <id> [--test <path>] --reason <r> [--worktree <p>] (no --test: the slice file alone, once every test it names is unfrozen)  | build pr <id> [--notes <file>] [--worktree <p>]  | build verdict <id> <file> [--independent] [--worktree <p>]  | build decline <id> <H-n> [--worktree <p>]  | build finish <id> [--wait <s>, default 90] [--worktree <p>]  | build sync <id> [--worktree <p>]

Each subcommand takes the slice ID, P<n>/S-<nn>. A slice's worktree is .worktrees/P<n>-S-<nn> on the branch slice/P<n>-S-<nn>-<descr>. --worktree <p> names the worktree to act in; without it the build worktree is used, never the review one.

SubcommandWhat it does
build nextPrints the first todo slice whose earlier phases and earlier Order steps are merged or released, and that no worktree or branch already holds.
build start <id>Makes the worktree and branch from the default branch, commits an empty claim and pushes it. Prints the worktree path, then the branch. For a slice this clone already started it prints resumed <path> at <state>.
build parallel P<n>Starts every runnable slice of the phase's next Order step, each in its own worktree. Prints <id> <worktree> <branch> per slice started.
build red <id> --tests <a,b>Runs the test command and requires it to fail, commits the tests alone, records them as frozen and moves the slice to building.
build commit <id> --message <m>Runs the tests, then commits with the test run's result and the Slice: trailer. With paths staged it commits those alone; with nothing staged, every changed path. It refuses a change to a frozen test or to a kit file. --require-green refuses unless every test passes.
build render <id>For a slice that changes the kit's own version: runs update --yes in the worktree and commits only the files it writes.
build config <id>For a slice whose Expected changes name .slicekit/config.json: commits the changed config alone.
build amend <id> [--test <path>] --reason <r>Unfreezes one frozen test after a person agreed and the slice file records it. With no --test it commits the slice file alone, once every test it names is unfrozen.
build pr <id> [--notes <file>]Runs the test, lint and build commands and check, pushes, opens the draft pull request or updates its body, and records draft-pr. Prints #<n> <url>, then verdict <file>.
build verdict <id> <file>Checks the reviewer's verdict file, commits it under .slicekit/reviews/, records in-review and pushes. Prints next: fix, ask, ci or stuck. --independent records an independent review's verdict, which does not count against the two rounds.
build decline <id> <H-n>Files one tracker issue for a declined should-have and adds its URL to the pull request body.
build finish <id> [--wait <s>]Waits for CI on the pull request's head. On green it marks the pull request ready for review and records ci-green, then ready when the ready-label decision passes.
build sync <id>Fast-forwards the worktree to its branch on origin and prints the new head.

build commit judges the slice's own state file before it runs a test. It refuses, with one line naming the state file, when the file is marked skip-worktree, when it is marked assume-unchanged, or when it differs on disk from the file at HEAD; the line says which of the three it found. No test runs and no commit is made. Clear the mark (git update-index --no-skip-worktree or --no-assume-unchanged) and restore the file from the last commit; only build commands write a state file, and each commits what it wrote.

With paths staged, build commit runs the test command in a temporary directory that holds the index as staged, so the command sees every tracked file as staged and no unstaged change. The files of the worktree that git ignores or does not track, such as node_modules or a list of test files, are readable there at the same relative path: a directory is linked and a file is linked or copied. A write the test command makes to a linked directory or a hard-linked file there changes the worktree's copy. A git command the test command runs in that directory exits 0 and reads the staged files. The directory is removed whether the run passes or fails, and removing it never walks into the worktree.

A machine that cannot run the whole test command at once can set testCommand in .slicekit/local.json. build red, build commit and build pr then use it and say so. CI never reads that file.

What it reads and writes

Reads the slice file, the slice's state file, the config, git and, for pr, verdict, decline and finish, the git host and the tracker. Writes commits on the slice branch, the state file under .slicekit/state/, verdict files under .slicekit/reviews/, the pull request and its body, and tracker issues. It never pushes a protected branch.

Exit codes
  • 0done; build commit with nothing to commit is success
  • 1refused: the slice's state, a failing command or check, a frozen test, a state file hidden from git or changed on disk, git, the git host, the tracker or a held lock; build next when no slice is ready; build verdict on next: stuck; build finish when CI failed, is still running or has no run
  • 2bad usage, an unknown slice ID, a missing required option, or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit build next
P1/S-02
$ slicekit build start P1/S-02
C:/work/orders/.worktrees/P1-S-02
slice/P1-S-02-place-order
$ slicekit build red P1/S-02 --tests test/order.test.js,test/order-empty.test.js
3f2a9c1…
tests-red → building
$ slicekit build commit P1/S-02 --message "feat(P1/S-02): place an order" --require-green
8b41d07 exit 0
$ slicekit build pr P1/S-02 --notes /tmp/slicekit-notes-P1-S-02.json
#14 https://github.com/acme/orders/pull/14
verdict C:/work/orders/P1-S-02-r1.md

Back to the guide

slicekit check

The kit's one gate: runs every check rule and prints each finding.

Usage
slicekit check [--ci] [--json]

Each finding is one line, <rule> <file>:<line> <message>. The last line is the summary, such as check: 0 findings, 0 over baseline, 0 blocking, 18 rules. A finding a ratchet baseline still allows is printed with (baseline) in front and does not fail the run.

  • --ci: adds what only CI can judge: the pull request's title and body, read from the GitHub event file, commit signatures, and the files of a sync pull request.
  • --json: prints one JSON document: findings, counts, over, blocking, exitCode and rules.

The rules, each with a page of its own:

RuleKindRunsWhat it checks
ci-bodyblockingonly under --ciUnder --ci, the pull request's body carries the sections the kit requires
ci-titleblockingonly under --ciUnder --ci, the pull request's title begins with the slice it delivers, and that slice was opened through the build loop
citationsblockingevery runEvery requirement cites a source that exists, every slice file names requirements and decisions that exist, and no ID is defined twice
commandsblockingevery runEvery command the team declared in the config can be found on this machine
coverageblockingevery runOnce a program is planned, every requirement belongs to a slice and every slice can be built and judged
frozenblockingevery runOn a slice branch, a test of the evaluation set stays as it was at the red commit
hooksblockingevery runThe git hooks the kit installs are present, executable and the ones git runs
host-rulesblockingevery runThe git host's rulesets on the default branch hold every rule the kit relies on
journalblockingevery runThe session journal is an unbroken, append-only record, and under --ci its commits are signed
layoutblockingevery runEvery file and folder slicekit init lays down is still there, and .claude/ holds no file of another shape
managedblockingevery runEvery file the kit renders still holds the block the kit wrote
queueblockingevery runBUILD.md reads exactly as the slice files and their state say
referencesratchetevery runEvery path, anchor and ID a doc names exists
runbookblockingevery runA slice that says it changes operations changes the runbook, or says why not
styleratchetevery runNo doc uses a phrase from the team's filler list
sync-releaseblockingonly under --ciUnder --ci on a sync pull request, the version, the changelog and the rendered files are exactly what CI computes for that merge
trailerblockingevery runOn a slice branch, every commit the branch adds names the slice in a Slice: trailer
workspaceblockingevery runA slice names a repository the workspace lists, and a contract names both of its parties

A rule that crashes, or whose ID another rule already took, is a blocking finding: the gate never passes because a rule did not run.

The Stop hook runs check when the agent tries to end a turn and blocks the turn while it is red. CI runs check --ci on every pull request. build pr runs it before every push.

What it reads and writes

Reads the config, every Markdown file under the docs root, BUILD.md, README.md, the verdicts and the rendered agent files, the slice and state files, the baselines and git. Under --ci it also reads the GitHub event file and the git host. It writes nothing; the sync-release rule uses a temporary worktree and removes it.

Exit codes
  • 0clean
  • 1a failing finding
  • 2cannot run: bad arguments or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit check
references docs/spec/refunds.md:9 missing file docs/spec/07-nothing.md
check: 1 findings, 1 over baseline, 1 blocking, 18 rules

Back to the guide

slicekit ci

Decides whether a push changes only the kit's bookkeeping, so CI can skip the team's commands.

Usage
slicekit ci bookkeeping [--base <sha>] [--head <sha>] [--base-branch <branch>] [--output <file>]

ci bookkeeping prints bookkeeping <base>..<head>, code <base>..<head> or code (<why>). Bookkeeping is state files, verdicts and BUILD.md. The team command jobs are skipped only on bookkeeping; any doubt is code.

  • --base <sha>: compare from this commit. Default: the newest commit of the pull request, at most 20 back, whose slicekit workflow run passed every team command job and which contains the base branch's tip. An empty or all-zero value means no base, so code.
  • --head <sha>: the commit to judge. Default: HEAD.
  • --base-branch <branch>: the branch the pull request merges into. Default: the config's default branch.
  • --output <file>: appends kind=bookkeeping or kind=code to this file, GitHub's step output.

The gate job of the generated workflow runs it first on every pull request push.

What it reads and writes

Reads git and, to search for a base, the git host's workflow runs. Writes only the --output file.

Exit codes
  • 0always, whatever the decision
  • 2bad usage
Example
$ slicekit ci bookkeeping --head "$SLICEKIT_PR_HEAD" --base-branch main --output "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
bookkeeping 8b41d07..a71c5e0

Back to the guide

slicekit decide

Writes a decision row outside the interview, or settles an open one.

Usage
slicekit decide add (--type <T> --question <q> --answer <a> | --open [--type <T>] --question <q> --why <w> --recommendation <r>) [--who <w>] [--replaces D-<n>] [--interface <name> [--source <file>:<line>]]slicekit decide settle D-<n> --answer <a> [--type <T>] [--who <w>]

decide add writes one row to <docsRoot>/decisions.md and prints its ID. A settled row is never rewritten: changing your mind is a new row with --replaces.

  • --type <T>: one of Decision, Action, Information, Counsel, Open. Required unless --open is given.
  • --question <q>: the question. Required.
  • --answer <a>: the answer, for a settled row.
  • --open: puts the row in the Open table; needs --why and --recommendation.
  • --who <w>: who decided. Default: git user.name, else unknown.
  • --replaces D-<n>: the settled row this one reverses.
  • --interface <name>: marks the row as naming an interface, so spec verify expects a contract for it. --source <file>:<line> says where the snapshot names it.

decide settle D-<n> --answer <a> moves an open row to the Settled table with its answer, keeping the same ID. --type <T> is required when the row's Type is Open.

What it reads and writes

Reads and writes <docsRoot>/decisions.md. It commits nothing.

Exit codes
  • 0prints the D-ID
  • 1a file problem (a missing file or table, wrong columns), or settle on a row already settled
  • 2bad usage, bad input or an unknown ID
Example
$ slicekit decide add --type Decision --question "Which database?" --answer "Postgres 16"
D-14
$ slicekit decide settle D-09 --answer "Stripe" --type Decision
D-09

Back to the guide

slicekit gaps

The steps of /slicekit gaps that the CLI takes: find gaps, record them, close them and verify the file.

Usage
slicekit gaps scanslicekit gaps verifyslicekit gaps add --class <c> --where <file>:<line> --what <text>slicekit gaps close G-<n> (--decision D-<n> | --req <REQ>)
SubcommandWhat it does
gaps scanAdds a row to <docsRoot>/spec/gaps.md for each gap a script can find: each "Not yet known" section, each open decision, each requirement that cites one, each interface with no contract. Prints the rows it added, or no new gaps.
gaps addWrites one open row and prints its G-ID. The auditor agent runs it for each gap a script cannot find. --class is one of missing, unsupported, contradiction, unknown, unrequested; --where is <file>:<line>; --what is one line. All three are required.
gaps close G-<n>Closes a row by naming what answered it: --decision D-<n>, a settled decision row, or --req <REQ>, a requirement changed on this branch that differs from the merged spec. Exactly one of the two.
gaps verifyChecks that every row is closed and no findable gap is missing. Prints ready: gap-scan, or one line per problem.
What it reads and writes

Reads the spec, the decisions, platform.md, observability.md and the runbook. scan, add and close write <docsRoot>/spec/gaps.md; verify writes nothing. None commits.

Exit codes
  • 0scanned, added, closed, or ready
  • 1a file problem, a row already closed, or a finding of gaps verify
  • 2bad usage, bad input, an unknown ID, or not exactly one of --decision and --req
Example
$ slicekit gaps scan
G-3 unknown D-09 is open: Which payment provider do refunds go through?
$ slicekit gaps close G-3 --decision D-09
G-3 closed by D-09
$ slicekit gaps verify
ready: gap-scan

Back to the guide

slicekit graph

Builds the traceability graph that the queries read.

Usage
slicekit graph [--full]

The graph is built from the kit's own IDs and from git: requirements, decisions, slices, tests, commits, pull requests and releases. It is not a code graph: it does not parse source code and infers no calls or imports.

The build is incremental: it walks only new commits and reads only changed files. graph is the only graph command that reads pull requests from the git host; without a host it skips them with a note. In a workspace of several repositories it walks each one. It prints the graph's path, the node and edge counts, what it walked and read, and each repository it could not reach.

  • --full: rebuilds from scratch, ignoring the saved index.

Run it before any query and after merges. The generated workflow builds the graph on every pull request and keeps it as an artifact.

A code graph alongside

For a code graph, graphify or a similar tool sits alongside the kit. This line installs graphify and its Claude Code skill:

pip install graphifyy && graphify install

Then one Claude Code session runs both: /graphify . for the code graph, then /slicekit build.

What it reads and writes

Reads the docs, the state files, the journal, git's history, the workspace file and, for pull requests, the git host. Writes .slicekit/graph/graph.json and its index beside it.

Exit codes
  • 0written
  • 1a schema problem, the default branch not present, or a bad workspace file
  • 2not a git repository, bad usage or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit graph
.slicekit/graph/graph.json
nodes 1240 edges 3315
commits walked 12 of 412
files read 9 of 188
pull requests fetched 2, from the cache 31

Back to the guide

slicekit history

Lists the slices whose commits touched the given paths.

Usage
slicekit history <path> [<path>…] [--json]

Newest first, each slice with its pull request, its last verdict and its release. Commits in no slice are not listed. A directory matches every file under it.

  • --json: prints one JSON document, also on an error ({"error": …}).

It answers "who changed this, under which slice, and was it reviewed?"

What it reads and writes

Reads only .slicekit/graph/graph.json. It runs no git and calls no host. It writes nothing.

Exit codes
  • 0answered
  • 1no graph (run slicekit graph), or a graph of an older schema
  • 2bad usage, an ID or path the graph does not hold, or a config problem
Example
$ slicekit history src/orders/place.js
P1/S-02  PR #14  APPROVE  unreleased

slicekit hook

Runs one Claude Code hook handler. Claude Code calls it; a person pipes JSON into it only to test a guard.

Usage
slicekit hook <name>

It reads a JSON object on stdin and prints one JSON decision.

NameClaude Code eventOn an error
session-startSessionStartanswers {}
pre-bashPreToolUse for Bashdenies the tool call
pre-editPreToolUse for Edit, Write, MultiEdit and NotebookEditdenies the tool call
subagent-startSubagentStartanswers {}
subagent-stopSubagentStopblocks the stop
pre-compactPreCompactanswers {}
stopStopblocks the stop
session-endSessionEndanswers {}

Outside a slicekit project every hook answers {}. init writes these commands into .claude/settings.json.

A hook never rewrites the config: one with an older configVersion is read as migrated, and the file is left as it is.

What it reads and writes

Reads stdin, the config, the state files and git. stop runs check. session-end appends one line to this clone's journal file. No hook writes the config.

Exit codes
  • 0for every known name; the decision is in the JSON
  • 2no name, or an unknown name
Example
$ echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git push --force origin main"},"cwd":"."}' | slicekit hook pre-bash

slicekit impact

Lists what shares files or contracts with a target.

Usage
slicekit impact <REQ-…|C-…|P<n>/S-<nn>|path> [--json]

The target is a requirement, a contract, a slice or a path; a directory matches every file under it. The answer lists the contracts, slices, files and repositories that share files or contracts with it. The kit's bookkeeping files never count, since every slice touches them.

  • --json: prints one JSON document, also on an error.

It answers "what else could this change break?"

What it reads and writes

Reads only .slicekit/graph/graph.json. It runs no git and calls no host. It writes nothing.

Exit codes
  • 0answered
  • 1no graph (run slicekit graph), or a graph of an older schema
  • 2bad usage, an ID or path the graph does not hold, or a config problem

  C-1 payments-api
